subject: Biology
title: Body Fluids and Circulation
summary: The chapter follows the fluids that carry material around the body: blood and its plasma, formed elements, blood groups and clotting; lymph; open and closed circulation and the evolution of the vertebrate heart; the structure of the human heart, its nodal tissue, the cardiac cycle, the ECG, double circulation, neural and hormonal regulation, and the common disorders. Almost every number, name and figure in it turns into a school-final question, and it is the base for the Class 12 chapters on immunity and for NEET, where one or two questions from it are near certain.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 11 Biology is a 70-mark theory paper set by the school on the CBSE pattern. Body Fluids and Circulation sits in Unit V, Human Physiology, the biggest unit of the year with about 18 marks spread over Breathing and Exchange of Gases, Body Fluids and Circulation, Excretory Products, Locomotion and Movement, Neural Control and Chemical Coordination. In a typical school final this chapter alone contributes 4 to 7 marks: one or two 1-mark items (an MCQ on RBC count, the pacemaker, universal donor, the QRS complex, or the animal with an open circulatory system, and an Assertion-Reason on erythroblastosis foetalis or the myogenic heart), a 2-mark or 3-mark question on blood groups, coagulation, lymph, heart sounds or the ECG, and every second year a 5-mark question that asks for a labelled section of the human heart with the cardiac cycle or double circulation. In NEET this chapter reliably gives one or two questions, nearly always taken straight from the NCERT numbers, Table 15.1 and the figures.

question_types.note: RBC count (5 to 5.5 million per mm<sup>3</sup>), haemoglobin (12 to 16 g per 100 mL), RBC life span (120 days) and graveyard (spleen); WBC count (6000 to 8000 per mm<sup>3</sup>) and the most abundant leucocyte (neutrophil); the leucocyte that secretes histamine, serotonin and heparin (basophil); platelets from megakaryocytes; universal donor (O) and universal recipient (AB); the enzyme that converts fibrinogen to fibrin (thrombin) and prothrombin to thrombin (thrombokinase); Rh antigen named after the rhesus monkey; open circulation in arthropods and molluscs; the 3-chambered heart of amphibians and reptiles except crocodiles; SAN as pacemaker in the right atrium; stroke volume 70 mL and cardiac output 5 L per min; P wave, QRS complex and T wave; lub and dub; blood pressure 120/80 and hypertension at 140/90; the difference between heart failure, cardiac arrest and heart attack.

The heart is myogenic because the nodal tissue is autoexcitable; SAN is the pacemaker because it generates the maximum number of action potentials; blood group O is the universal donor because its RBCs carry no antigen; erythroblastosis foetalis affects the second Rh-positive foetus because antibodies formed after the first delivery cross the placenta; the first heart sound is due to closure of the atrio-ventricular valves; closed circulation is more advantageous because flow can be precisely regulated; the ECG cannot show the atrial repolarisation because it is masked by the QRS complex; fibrinogen does not clot blood in an intact vessel because thrombin is present only as inactive prothrombin.

Why blood is a connective tissue; the difference between plasma and serum; two functions of plasma proteins; name the granulocytes and agranulocytes; define cardiac output and give its value; name the two heart sounds and their causes; why the heart is called myogenic; what the P, QRS and T waves mean; two differences between open and closed circulation; two differences between blood and lymph; define double circulation; name the fluids absorbed through the lacteals.

Describe the formed elements with one function each; explain the ABO system with Table 15.1; explain erythroblastosis foetalis and how it is prevented; write the cascade of blood coagulation; explain the cardiac cycle in three stages; describe the conducting system of the heart; explain the standard ECG with a diagram; give the neural and hormonal regulation of cardiac activity; explain three disorders of the circulatory system; trace the evolution of the vertebrate heart.

Draw a labelled section of the human heart and describe its chambers, septa and valves; explain double circulation with a schematic diagram and its significance; describe the cardiac cycle with the events in atria, ventricles and valves, and calculate cardiac output; draw and explain the standard ECG and its use in diagnosis; describe blood as a tissue covering plasma, formed elements and their counts and functions.

A blood report with counts of RBCs, WBCs and platelets from a dengue patient; a table of ABO groups with questions on safe transfusion; a passage on an Rh-negative mother in her second pregnancy; an ECG trace with sub-questions on the waves and on counting heart rate; a passage on a middle-aged man with chest pain, high BP and narrowed coronary arteries; a passage on an athlete with high stroke volume and low resting rate.

sections.heading: Introduction: why the body needs circulating fluids
sections.body:
Every living cell needs nutrients, O2 and other essential substances brought to it, and needs its waste and harmful substances taken away. In a single cell or a thin animal, simple diffusion across the surface is enough. In a large animal the inner cells are far from the surface, so the body uses fluids that move through it and act as a medium of transport. This is the whole point of the chapter and NCERT states it in the first paragraph: complex organisms use special fluids within their bodies to transport such materials.

Two body fluids are commonly used by higher organisms. Blood is the most commonly used, and lymph (tissue fluid) helps in the transport of certain substances. Sponges and coelenterates do without either; they circulate water from their surroundings through their body cavities to move nutrients and gases. Everything that follows is organised around these two fluids and the pump that moves blood.

Read the chapter in NCERT order, because school papers follow the same order: first what blood is made of (plasma, formed elements, blood groups, clotting), then lymph, then the two patterns of circulation in animals and how the vertebrate heart evolved, then the human heart in detail (structure, nodal tissue, cardiac cycle, ECG, double circulation, regulation), and finally the disorders. The examiner rewards the exact NCERT terms and numbers, so keep a list of every count and value as you go; the formula sheet at the end of this guide collects them.
sections.tip: If a 1-mark question asks how sponges and coelenterates transport materials, the answer is that they circulate water from their surroundings through their body cavities, not blood.

sections.heading: 15.1 Blood and 15.1.1 Plasma
sections.body:
Blood is a special connective tissue consisting of a fluid matrix, plasma, and formed elements. It is called a connective tissue because, like every connective tissue, it has cells lying in a matrix; in blood the matrix happens to be fluid and has no fibres except during clotting. When a question asks 'why is blood considered a connective tissue', write exactly that: it is mesodermal in origin, its cells (formed elements) are scattered in a non-living matrix (plasma), and it connects different parts of the body by transporting materials between them.

Plasma is a straw-coloured, viscous fluid constituting nearly 55 per cent of the blood. It is 90 to 92 per cent water and 6 to 8 per cent proteins. The plasma proteins are of three kinds: fibrinogen, globulins and albumins. Fibrinogens are needed for clotting or coagulation of blood. Globulins are involved primarily in defence mechanisms of the body (antibodies are gamma globulins). Albumins help in osmotic balance, holding water inside the vessels. Small amounts of minerals like Na+, Ca2+, Mg2+, HCO3− and Cl− are also present in plasma, along with glucose, amino acids and lipids, which are always in transit in the body.

One more sentence from NCERT matters: factors for coagulation or clotting of blood are also present in the plasma in an inactive form. Plasma without the clotting factors is called serum. So the 2-mark difference between plasma and serum is simply this: plasma is the whole fluid part of blood and contains fibrinogen and the other clotting factors; serum is what is left after blood has clotted, so it lacks fibrinogen and the clotting factors but still has albumins, globulins, minerals and nutrients.
sections.tip: Write the three plasma proteins with one function each: fibrinogen for clotting, globulins for defence, albumins for osmotic balance. A list without functions loses half the marks.

sections.heading: 15.1.2 Formed Elements
sections.body:
Erythrocytes, leucocytes and platelets are collectively called formed elements and they constitute nearly 45 per cent of the blood. The counts, sites of formation and functions in this section are the most heavily examined facts of the chapter.

Erythrocytes (RBCs) are the most abundant of all the cells in blood. A healthy adult man has, on an average, 5 million to 5.5 million RBCs per mm3 of blood. RBCs are formed in the red bone marrow in adults. In most mammals they are devoid of nucleus and are biconcave in shape; the lost nucleus leaves the whole cell volume for haemoglobin, and the biconcave shape increases the surface for gas exchange. They have a red-coloured, iron-containing complex protein called haemoglobin, and a healthy person has 12 to 16 g of haemoglobin in every 100 mL of blood. Haemoglobin plays a significant role in the transport of respiratory gases. RBCs have an average life span of 120 days, after which they are destroyed in the spleen, which is therefore called the graveyard of RBCs.

Leucocytes (WBCs) are colourless due to the lack of haemoglobin, and they are nucleated. They are relatively few, 6000 to 8000 per mm3, and are generally short-lived. There are two main categories. Granulocytes are neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils. Agranulocytes are lymphocytes and monocytes. Learn the percentages: neutrophils 60 to 65 per cent (the most abundant), lymphocytes 20 to 25 per cent, monocytes 6 to 8 per cent, eosinophils 2 to 3 per cent, basophils 0.5 to 1 per cent (the least abundant). Neutrophils and monocytes are phagocytic cells that destroy foreign organisms entering the body. Basophils secrete histamine, serotonin and heparin and are involved in inflammatory reactions. Eosinophils resist infections and are also associated with allergic reactions. Lymphocytes are of two major types, B and T forms, and both are responsible for immune responses of the body.

Platelets, also called thrombocytes, are cell fragments produced from megakaryocytes (special cells in the bone marrow). Blood normally contains 1.5 lakh to 3.5 lakh platelets per mm3. Platelets release a variety of substances, most of which are involved in the coagulation or clotting of blood. A reduction in their number can lead to clotting disorders and excessive loss of blood from the body; this is why a dengue report is watched for its platelet count.
sections.tip: NCERT's exact match: neutrophils and monocytes phagocytic; basophils histamine, serotonin, heparin; eosinophils allergy; lymphocytes B and T. A question that swaps basophil and eosinophil is the commonest 1-mark trap in this chapter.

sections.heading: 15.1.3 Blood Groups: ABO and Rh
sections.body:
The blood of all humans looks alike but differs in certain aspects, and two groupings are widely used: the ABO system and the Rh system. Both matter because transfusing the wrong blood makes the recipient's antibodies clump (agglutinate) and destroy the donor's RBCs.

ABO grouping is based on the presence or absence of two surface antigens (chemicals that can induce an immune response) on the RBCs, namely antigen A and antigen B. Similarly, the plasma of different individuals contains two natural antibodies (proteins produced in response to antigens). The distribution is Table 15.1 of NCERT and you must reproduce it from memory. Group A: antigen A on RBCs, antibody anti-B in plasma, can receive from A and O. Group B: antigen B, antibody anti-A, can receive from B and O. Group AB: antigens A and B, no antibodies, can receive from AB, A, B and O. Group O: no antigen, antibodies anti-A and anti-B, can receive from O only. Because group O has no antigens, its blood can be donated to persons with any other blood group, so O is the universal donor. Because group AB has no antibodies, persons with AB can accept blood from any group, so AB is the universal recipient. The logic to write in the exam: the donor's RBC antigen must not meet a matching antibody in the recipient's plasma.

Rh grouping: another antigen, the Rh antigen, similar to one present in Rhesus monkeys, is observed on the surface of RBCs of majority (nearly 80 per cent) of humans. Such individuals are called Rh positive (Rh+ve) and those in whom this antigen is absent are Rh negative (Rh−ve). An Rh−ve person, if exposed to Rh+ve blood, forms specific antibodies against the Rh antigen, so Rh group should also be matched before transfusion.

The examiner's favourite case is erythroblastosis foetalis: a special case of Rh incompatibility between the Rh−ve mother and the Rh+ve foetus. In the first pregnancy the Rh antigens of the foetus do not get exposed to the mother's blood, because the two bloods are well separated by the placenta. During the delivery of the first child, however, there is a possibility of exposure of the maternal blood to small amounts of Rh+ve blood from the foetus. The mother then starts preparing antibodies against the Rh antigen. In a subsequent pregnancy with an Rh+ve foetus, these antibodies can leak into the blood of the foetus and destroy its RBCs, causing severe anaemia and jaundice in the baby; the condition can be fatal. It can be avoided by administering anti-Rh antibodies to the mother immediately after the delivery of the first child, which mop up the foetal Rh antigens before the mother's immune system is sensitised.
sections.tip: Always say 'Rh-negative mother, Rh-positive foetus, second pregnancy'. Students who write that the first child is affected, or that the mother is Rh-positive, lose the mark.

sections.heading: 15.1.4 Coagulation of Blood
sections.body:
Blood exhibits coagulation or clotting in response to an injury or trauma; this is a mechanism to prevent excessive loss of blood from the body. A dark reddish brown scum forms at the site of a cut, and that is the clot.

NCERT describes the clot precisely, and the wording earns marks: the clot or coagulum is formed mainly of a network of threads called fibrins, in which dead and damaged formed elements of blood are trapped. Fibrins are formed by the conversion of inactive fibrinogens in the plasma by the enzyme thrombin. Thrombins, in turn, are formed from another inactive substance present in the plasma, prothrombin. An enzyme complex, thrombokinase, is required for this conversion. This complex is formed by a series of linked enzymic reactions, a cascade process, involving a number of factors present in the plasma in an inactive state. An injury or trauma stimulates the platelets in the blood to release certain factors which activate the mechanism of coagulation; certain factors released by the tissues at the site of injury can also initiate coagulation. Calcium ions play a very important role in clotting.

The three-step cascade to write, in order, as a flow chart:

  1. Injury: platelets and damaged tissue release factors → inactive plasma factors are activated one after another → the enzyme complex thrombokinase is formed.
  2. Thrombokinase, with Ca2+, converts inactive prothrombin into active thrombin.
  3. Thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads; the network traps formed elements and forms the clot.

Two related facts are often asked from outside the strict NCERT text but from its logic. Blood does not clot inside an intact vessel because thrombin does not exist there (only inactive prothrombin), the endothelium is smooth, and heparin from basophils acts as an anticoagulant. In a blood bank, blood is kept from clotting by adding sodium citrate or oxalate, which removes Ca2+; EDTA works the same way. A deficiency of vitamin K delays clotting because prothrombin is synthesised in the liver with vitamin K.
sections.tip: Write the cascade with arrows and name the enzyme at each step: thrombokinase (with Ca<sup>2+</sup>) for prothrombin → thrombin, thrombin for fibrinogen → fibrin. Naming the products without the enzymes loses marks.

sections.heading: 15.2 Lymph (Tissue Fluid)
sections.body:
As blood passes through the capillaries in the tissues, some water along with many small water-soluble substances moves out into the spaces between the cells of tissues, leaving the larger proteins and most of the formed elements in the blood vessels. This fluid released out is called the interstitial fluid or tissue fluid. It has the same mineral distribution as that in plasma, and it is the medium through which exchange of nutrients, gases and other substances between the blood and the cells actually takes place.

An elaborate network of vessels, the lymphatic system, collects this fluid and drains it back to the major veins. The fluid present in the lymphatic system is called lymph. Lymph is a colourless fluid containing specialised lymphocytes, which are responsible for the immune responses of the body. Lymph is also an important carrier for nutrients, hormones and so on. Fats are absorbed through lymph in the lacteals present in the intestinal villi, which is why lymph draining from the intestine after a fatty meal looks milky (chyle).

The 2-mark and 3-mark question on this section is the comparison of blood and lymph. Blood is red because of haemoglobin in RBCs; lymph is colourless because it has no RBCs. Blood has RBCs, all types of WBCs and platelets; lymph has only leucocytes, mainly lymphocytes, and no platelets. Blood plasma has more proteins, including fibrinogen; lymph has less protein and clots slowly. Blood flows in a closed loop from the heart and back; lymph flows only in one direction, from the tissues towards the heart, driven by muscle movement and valves, and joins the venous blood. Blood carries O2, CO2, nutrients and wastes throughout the body; lymph returns tissue fluid and proteins to the blood, carries absorbed fats and provides immunity.
sections.tip: For 'fats are absorbed through lymph', name the vessel: lacteals in the intestinal villi. That one word is usually the marking point.

sections.heading: 15.3 Circulatory Pathways and the evolution of the vertebrate heart
sections.body:
The circulatory patterns are of two types, open or closed. An open circulatory system is present in arthropods and molluscs: blood pumped by the heart passes through large vessels into open spaces or body cavities called sinuses, bathing the organs directly. Annelids and chordates have a closed circulatory system, in which the blood pumped by the heart is always circulated through a closed network of blood vessels. This pattern is considered more advantageous because the flow of fluid can be more precisely regulated: blood can be directed to the organs that need it, at a controlled pressure and speed.

All vertebrates possess a muscular chambered heart, and the chapter traces its evolution. Fishes have a 2-chambered heart with one atrium and one ventricle. Amphibians and reptiles (except crocodiles) have a 3-chambered heart with two atria and a single ventricle. Crocodiles, birds and mammals possess a 4-chambered heart with two atria and two ventricles.

In fishes the heart pumps out deoxygenated blood, which is oxygenated by the gills and supplied to the body parts, from where deoxygenated blood is returned to the heart. Blood passes through the heart only once per circuit: single circulation. In amphibians and reptiles, the left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the gills, lungs or skin, and the right atrium gets the deoxygenated blood from other body parts. However, they get mixed up in the single ventricle, which pumps out mixed blood: incomplete double circulation. In birds and mammals, oxygenated and deoxygenated blood received by the left and right atria respectively pass on to the ventricles of the same sides; the ventricles pump it out without any mixing, so two separate circulatory pathways are present: double circulation.

When the exercise asks you to describe the evolutionary change in the pattern of heart among vertebrates, write these three stages with the number of chambers, the example animals, and the consequence for mixing of blood. The examiner is looking for the trend: from a single circuit with a two-chambered heart, through partial separation with three chambers, to complete separation with four chambers and no mixing, which supports the high metabolic rate of endothermic birds and mammals.
sections.tip: Remember the exception: crocodiles are reptiles but have a four-chambered heart. A question that lists 'all reptiles' as three-chambered is wrong for that reason.

sections.heading: 15.3.1 Human Circulatory System: the heart and its conducting tissue
sections.body:
The human circulatory system, also called the blood vascular system, consists of a muscular chambered heart, a network of closed branching blood vessels, and blood. The heart is mesodermally derived, situated in the thoracic cavity, in between the two lungs, slightly tilted to the left, and is about the size of a clenched fist. It is protected by a double-walled membranous bag, the pericardium, enclosing the pericardial fluid, which reduces friction as the heart beats.

The heart has four chambers: two relatively small upper chambers, the atria, and two larger lower chambers, the ventricles. A thin muscular wall, the inter-atrial septum, separates the right and left atria; a thick-walled inter-ventricular septum separates the left and right ventricles. The atrium and ventricle of the same side are separated by a thick fibrous tissue, the atrio-ventricular septum, with an opening on each side through which the two chambers of that side are connected. The opening between the right atrium and right ventricle is guarded by the tricuspid valve, formed of three muscular flaps or cusps; the opening between the left atrium and left ventricle is guarded by the bicuspid or mitral valve. The openings of the right and left ventricles into the pulmonary artery and the aorta respectively are provided with semilunar valves. All these valves allow the flow of blood in one direction only, from the atria to the ventricles and from the ventricles to the pulmonary artery or aorta, and prevent any backward flow. The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it pumps blood to the whole body.

The entire heart is made of cardiac muscles. The walls of the ventricles are much thicker than those of the atria. A specialised cardiac musculature called the nodal tissue is also distributed in the heart. A patch of this tissue is present in the right upper corner of the right atrium, the sino-atrial node (SAN); another mass is in the lower left corner of the right atrium close to the atrio-ventricular septum, the atrio-ventricular node (AVN). A bundle of nodal fibres, the atrio-ventricular bundle (AV bundle, bundle of His), continues from the AVN, passes through the atrio-ventricular septa to emerge on the top of the inter-ventricular septum, and immediately divides into a right and a left bundle. These branches give rise to minute fibres throughout the ventricular musculature of the respective sides, the Purkinje fibres.

The nodal musculature has the ability to generate action potentials without any external stimuli: it is autoexcitable. The number of action potentials that could be generated in a minute varies at different parts of the nodal system. The SAN can generate the maximum, 70 to 75 per minute, and is responsible for initiating and maintaining the rhythmic contractile activity of the heart; so it is called the pacemaker. Our heart normally beats 70 to 75 times in a minute, average 72 beats per minute. Because the impulse originates in the muscle itself and not in a nerve, the heart is called myogenic; the heart of a cockroach or an annelid, whose beat is started by nerves, is neurogenic.
sections.tip: For 'why is SAN called the pacemaker', two points earn the marks: it generates the maximum number of action potentials (70 to 75 per minute), and it initiates and maintains the rhythmic contraction of the heart. Its location, right upper corner of the right atrium, is the third.

sections.heading: 15.4 Cardiac Cycle
sections.body:
NCERT explains the cycle by starting from the moment when all four chambers are relaxed, the joint diastole. At this time the tricuspid and bicuspid valves are open, so blood from the pulmonary veins and the venae cavae flows into the left and right atria respectively and passes straight on into the ventricles; the semilunar valves are closed.

The SAN now generates an action potential which stimulates both atria to undergo simultaneous contraction, the atrial systole. This increases the flow of blood into the ventricles by about 30 per cent; that is, most ventricular filling happens passively during diastole, and the atrial kick tops it up. The action potential is conducted to the ventricular side through the AVN and AV bundle and then to the ventricular musculature by the Purkinje fibres, so the ventricles contract: ventricular systole. The atria meanwhile relax (atrial diastole), coinciding with ventricular systole. Ventricular systole increases the ventricular pressure, causing the closure of the tricuspid and bicuspid valves due to the attempted backflow of blood into the atria. As the ventricular pressure increases further, the semilunar valves guarding the pulmonary artery (right side) and the aorta (left side) are forced open, allowing blood in the ventricles to flow through these vessels into the circulatory pathways. The ventricles now relax (ventricular diastole) and the ventricular pressure falls, causing the closure of the semilunar valves, which prevents the backflow of blood into the ventricles. As the ventricular pressure declines further, the tricuspid and bicuspid valves open and blood from the atria, which is already being filled from the veins, flows into the ventricles. The ventricles and atria are now again in a relaxed (joint diastole) state.

This sequential event in the heart, which is cyclically repeated, is called the cardiac cycle, and it consists of systole and diastole of both the atria and ventricles. The heart beats 72 times per minute, so that many cardiac cycles are performed per minute, and the duration of one cardiac cycle is 0.8 second. Teachers usually split it as atrial systole 0.1 s, ventricular systole 0.3 s and joint diastole 0.4 s; NCERT gives only the total, so quote the total and add the split as a bonus.

During a cardiac cycle each ventricle pumps out approximately 70 mL of blood, called the stroke volume. The stroke volume multiplied by the heart rate (number of beats per minute) gives the cardiac output: 70 mL × 72 = about 5000 mL or 5 litres per minute in a normal adult. The body has the ability to alter the stroke volume as well as the heart rate and thereby the cardiac output; the cardiac output of an athlete is much higher than that of an ordinary man.

During each cardiac cycle two prominent sounds are produced, which can be easily heard through a stethoscope. The first heart sound, lub, is associated with the closure of the tricuspid and bicuspid valves at the start of ventricular systole; the second, dub, is associated with the closure of the semilunar valves at the start of ventricular diastole. These sounds are of clinical diagnostic significance: a murmur points to a leaking or narrowed valve.

formulas.expr: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate = 70 mL × 72 per min ≈ 5000 mL per min (5 L per min)
where: blood pumped by each ventricle per beat, about 70 mL
beats per minute, normally 70 to 75, average 72

formulas.expr: Duration of one cardiac cycle = 60 s ÷ 72 ≈ 0.8 s
where: atrial systole 0.1 s + ventricular systole 0.3 s + joint diastole 0.4 s in the usual teaching split

sections.tip: Lub is the AV valves closing, dub is the semilunar valves closing. Write which valves, not 'first sound at systole', because the valve name is the marking point.

sections.heading: 15.5 Electrocardiograph (ECG)
sections.body:
An electrocardiograph is the machine, and the electrocardiogram (ECG) is the graphical representation of the electrical activity of the heart during a cardiac cycle that it records. To obtain a standard ECG, a patient is connected to the machine with three electrical leads (one to each wrist and one to the left ankle) that continuously monitor the heart activity. For a detailed evaluation of the heart's function, multiple leads are attached to the chest region. The chapter asks you to understand only the standard ECG, which is Fig. 15.4.

Each peak in the ECG is identified with a letter from P to T, corresponding to a specific electrical activity of the heart. The P wave represents the electrical excitation (depolarisation) of the atria, which leads to the contraction of both the atria. The QRS complex represents the depolarisation of the ventricles, which initiates the ventricular contraction; the contraction starts shortly after Q and marks the beginning of the systole. The T wave represents the return of the ventricles from the excited to the normal state (repolarisation); the end of the T wave marks the end of systole. Atrial repolarisation also happens, but it is masked by the large QRS complex and does not appear as a separate wave.

Two practical points are asked. First, since the ECGs obtained from different individuals have roughly the same shape for a given lead configuration, any deviation from this shape indicates a possible abnormality or disease; hence it has great clinical significance. Second, by counting the number of QRS complexes that occur in a given time period, one can determine the heart beat rate of an individual. If a strip shows 6 QRS complexes in 5 seconds, the heart rate is 6 × 12 = 72 per minute.

When you draw the ECG, plot voltage against time as a baseline with a small rounded P bump, a sharp downward Q, a tall narrow upward R, a small downward S and then a broad rounded T. Label the five letters and write against them 'atrial depolarisation', 'ventricular depolarisation' and 'ventricular repolarisation'. Mark the P-Q interval as the time taken for the impulse to travel from the atria through the AVN to the ventricles, and the S-T segment as the plateau when the ventricles are fully depolarised.

formulas.expr: Heart rate (per min) = number of QRS complexes in t seconds × (60 ÷ t)
where: one per ventricular depolarisation, so one per heart beat

sections.tip: The word for P and QRS is depolarisation, the word for T is repolarisation. Writing 'contraction' and 'relaxation' alone is accepted less often than the electrical terms.

sections.heading: 15.6 Double Circulation
sections.body:
The blood pumped by the right ventricle enters the pulmonary artery, whereas the left ventricle pumps blood into the aorta. The deoxygenated blood pumped into the pulmonary artery is passed on to the lungs, from where the oxygenated blood is carried by the pulmonary veins into the left atrium. This pathway constitutes the pulmonary circulation. The oxygenated blood entering the aorta is carried by a network of arteries, arterioles and capillaries to the tissues, from where the deoxygenated blood is collected by a system of venules, veins and venae cavae and emptied into the right atrium. This is the systemic circulation. The systemic circulation provides nutrients, O2 and other essential substances to the tissues and takes CO2 and other harmful substances away for elimination.

Because the blood goes through the heart twice in one complete circuit, once through the right side on its way to the lungs and once through the left side on its way to the body, the circulation is called double circulation. Its significance, which is a standard 2-mark question: oxygenated and deoxygenated blood are kept completely separate, so the tissues receive fully oxygenated blood at high pressure, which supports the high metabolic rate and constant body temperature of birds and mammals; and the lungs receive blood at a lower pressure suited to the delicate alveolar capillaries.

Two special circuits are named in NCERT. A unique vascular connection exists between the digestive tract and the liver, the hepatic portal system: the hepatic portal vein carries blood from the intestine to the liver before it is delivered to the systemic circulation, so absorbed nutrients are processed and toxins removed first. A special coronary system of blood vessels is present in our body exclusively for the circulation of blood to and from the cardiac musculature; blockage of a coronary artery is what causes a heart attack.

The schematic plan of Fig. 15.5 should be written as one flow: body tissues → superior and inferior venae cavae → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → bicuspid valve → left ventricle → aorta → body tissues. Note the two counter-intuitive vessel names: the pulmonary artery is the only artery carrying deoxygenated blood, and the pulmonary veins are the only veins carrying oxygenated blood.
sections.tip: A 'define double circulation' answer needs the phrase 'blood passes twice through the heart in one complete circuit' and the names of the two circuits, pulmonary and systemic.

sections.heading: 15.7 Regulation of Cardiac Activity
sections.body:
Normal activities of the heart are regulated intrinsically, that is, auto-regulated by specialised muscles (nodal tissue); hence the heart is called myogenic. The SAN sets the basic rhythm without any input from the nervous system, which is why an isolated heart kept in a suitable solution keeps beating. The nervous and endocrine systems only adjust this rhythm up or down.

A special neural centre in the medulla oblongata can moderate the cardiac function through the autonomic nervous system (ANS). Neural signals through the sympathetic nerves (part of the ANS) can increase the rate of heart beat, the strength of ventricular contraction and thereby the cardiac output; this is the fight-or-flight adjustment during exercise, fear or blood loss. On the other hand, parasympathetic neural signals (another component of the ANS, carried by the vagus nerve) decrease the rate of heart beat, the speed of conduction of the action potential and thereby the cardiac output; this is the rest-and-digest setting. Adrenal medullary hormones, adrenaline and noradrenaline, can also increase the cardiac output, which is why the heart races before an exam.

Put the three influences in one table when you answer: nodal tissue sets the rhythm (myogenic); sympathetic nerves and adrenal medullary hormones speed it up and strengthen it; parasympathetic nerves slow it down. A common 2-mark question is 'why is the heart called myogenic even though it is innervated'. The answer: the rhythm originates in the heart's own nodal tissue, which is autoexcitable, and the nerves only modify the rate; a denervated or transplanted heart still beats.
sections.tip: Sympathetic increases rate, force and cardiac output; parasympathetic decreases rate, conduction speed and cardiac output. NCERT lists these exact three effects on each side; write all three.

sections.heading: 15.8 Disorders of Circulatory System
sections.body:
High blood pressure (hypertension) is the term for blood pressure that is higher than normal. Normal blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg: 120 is the systolic pressure, the pressure in the arteries when the ventricles contract, and 80 is the diastolic pressure, the pressure when the ventricles relax. If repeated checks of blood pressure of an individual are 140/90 mm Hg or higher, it shows hypertension. High blood pressure leads to heart diseases and also affects vital organs like the brain and kidney.

Coronary artery disease (CAD), often referred to as atherosclerosis, affects the vessels that supply blood to the heart muscle. It is caused by deposits of calcium, fat, cholesterol and fibrous tissues in the coronary arteries, which make the lumen of the arteries narrower and reduce the blood supply to the cardiac muscle.

Angina pectoris, or simply angina, is a symptom of acute chest pain that appears when not enough oxygen is reaching the heart muscle. It can occur in men and women of any age but is more common among the middle-aged and elderly. It occurs because blood flow to the heart is affected, typically by narrowed coronary arteries during exertion.

Heart failure is the state of the heart when it is not pumping blood effectively enough to meet the needs of the body. It is sometimes called congestive heart failure because congestion of the lungs is one of its main symptoms. The examiner likes the three-way distinction from the NCERT paragraph: heart failure is not the same as cardiac arrest (when the heart stops beating) or a heart attack (when the heart muscle is suddenly damaged by an inadequate blood supply). Write all three as one-line definitions in a 3-mark question and you will get full marks.

For the case-study style question, connect the four: fatty deposits cause atherosclerosis (CAD); the narrowed lumen reduces O2 to the myocardium, felt as angina; a complete block kills part of the muscle, a heart attack; a weakened heart that cannot meet demand is in heart failure; and hypertension accelerates all of this by damaging the artery walls.
sections.tip: Learn the two numbers: normal 120/80, hypertension 140/90 or above on repeated checks. Say 'repeated checks'; a single high reading is not hypertension.

key_terms.definition: The straw-coloured, viscous fluid matrix of blood, about 55 per cent of blood volume, made of 90 to 92 per cent water and 6 to 8 per cent proteins (fibrinogen, globulins, albumins) with minerals, nutrients and inactive clotting factors.
Plasma from which the clotting factors, especially fibrinogen, have been removed; it is the fluid left after blood has clotted.
The erythrocytes, leucocytes and platelets of blood, which together make up nearly 45 per cent of blood volume.

Red blood cells, 5 to 5.5 million per mm<sup>3</sup>, biconcave, enucleate in most mammals, formed in red bone marrow, filled with haemoglobin (12 to 16 g per 100 mL), living about 120 days before destruction in the spleen.
The two categories of leucocytes: granulocytes are neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils; agranulocytes are lymphocytes and monocytes.
Cell fragments produced from megakaryocytes of the bone marrow, 1.5 to 3.5 lakh per mm<sup>3</sup>, releasing substances involved in coagulation.

An antigen is a chemical that can induce an immune response, such as antigen A or B on the RBC surface; an antibody is a protein produced in response to an antigen, such as anti-A or anti-B in plasma.
Group O, whose RBCs carry no antigen, can donate to any ABO group (universal donor); group AB, whose plasma has no antibodies, can receive from any group (universal recipient).
An antigen on the RBC surface, similar to one in Rhesus monkeys, present in nearly 80 per cent of humans (Rh positive) and absent in the rest (Rh negative).

Rh incompatibility between an Rh-negative mother and an Rh-positive foetus in which maternal anti-Rh antibodies, formed after the first delivery, destroy the RBCs of a later Rh-positive foetus, causing severe anaemia and jaundice; prevented by giving anti-Rh antibodies to the mother just after the first delivery.

Clotting of blood in response to injury: a cascade of plasma factors forms thrombokinase, which with Ca<sup>2+</sup> converts prothrombin to thrombin, which converts fibrinogen to fibrin threads that trap formed elements as a clot.

The colourless fluid of the lymphatic system, formed from interstitial (tissue) fluid, containing specialised lymphocytes; it carries nutrients and hormones and absorbs fats through the lacteals of intestinal villi.

In open circulation (arthropods, molluscs) blood pumped by the heart flows through large vessels into open sinuses; in closed circulation (annelids, chordates) blood always stays within a closed network of vessels, which allows more precise regulation of flow.
The double-walled membranous bag enclosing the heart and the pericardial fluid, which protects the heart and reduces friction.

The patch of nodal tissue in the right upper corner of the right atrium that generates the maximum number of action potentials (70 to 75 per minute) and so initiates and maintains the heart's rhythm; the pacemaker.

key_terms.term: Atrio-ventricular node and bundle of His
key_terms.definition: The AVN in the lower left corner of the right atrium receives the impulse from the atria and passes it through the AV bundle (bundle of His), its right and left branches and the Purkinje fibres to the ventricular muscle.
A heart whose beat originates in its own specialised muscle (nodal tissue), not in nerves; the human heart is myogenic, the nervous system only modifies its rate.
The sequence of systole and diastole of both atria and both ventricles that is cyclically repeated; one cycle lasts about 0.8 s at 72 beats per minute.
Stroke volume is the blood pumped by each ventricle per beat (about 70 mL); cardiac output is stroke volume times heart rate, about 5000 mL or 5 L per minute.
The graphical record of the electrical activity of the heart during a cardiac cycle: P wave (atrial depolarisation), QRS complex (ventricular depolarisation), T wave (ventricular repolarisation).

The pattern in birds and mammals in which blood passes through the heart twice per circuit, once through the pulmonary circulation (right heart to lungs to left atrium) and once through the systemic circulation (left heart to body to right atrium), with no mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.
The vascular connection in which the hepatic portal vein carries blood from the intestine to the liver before it joins the systemic circulation.
Blood pressure persistently at or above 140/90 mm Hg on repeated checks, against a normal of 120/80 mm Hg; it leads to heart disease and damages the brain and kidney.
Narrowing of the coronary arteries by deposits of calcium, fat, cholesterol and fibrous tissue, reducing blood supply to the heart muscle.
Acute chest pain that appears when not enough oxygen reaches the heart muscle because blood flow to the heart is reduced.

The state in which the heart is not pumping blood effectively enough to meet the body's needs; called congestive heart failure when lung congestion is a main symptom; distinct from cardiac arrest (heart stops) and heart attack (muscle damaged by inadequate supply).

formula_sheet.name: Blood composition
formula_sheet.expr: Plasma 55 per cent (90 to 92 per cent water, 6 to 8 per cent proteins: fibrinogen, globulins, albumins); formed elements 45 per cent
formula_sheet.note: Serum = plasma minus clotting factors. Minerals in plasma: Na<sup>+</sup>, Ca<sup>2+</sup>, Mg<sup>2+</sup>, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>, Cl<sup>−</sup>.

formula_sheet.name: RBC facts
formula_sheet.expr: 5 to 5.5 million per mm<sup>3</sup>; haemoglobin 12 to 16 g per 100 mL; biconcave, enucleate in most mammals; formed in red bone marrow; life span 120 days; destroyed in spleen
formula_sheet.note: Spleen is the graveyard of RBCs. Enucleate so the entire cell volume carries haemoglobin.

formula_sheet.name: WBC facts
formula_sheet.expr: 6000 to 8000 per mm<sup>3</sup>; neutrophils 60 to 65 per cent, lymphocytes 20 to 25 per cent, monocytes 6 to 8 per cent, eosinophils 2 to 3 per cent, basophils 0.5 to 1 per cent
formula_sheet.note: Neutrophils and monocytes phagocytic; basophils release histamine, serotonin, heparin (inflammation); eosinophils resist infection, allergy; lymphocytes B and T, immunity.

formula_sheet.name: Platelet facts
formula_sheet.expr: 1.5 lakh to 3.5 lakh per mm<sup>3</sup>; cell fragments from megakaryocytes in bone marrow; release clotting factors
formula_sheet.note: Low count (as in dengue) causes bleeding and clotting disorders.

formula_sheet.name: ABO groups (Table 15.1)
formula_sheet.expr: A: antigen A, anti-B, receives A and O; B: antigen B, anti-A, receives B and O; AB: antigens A and B, no antibody, receives all (universal recipient); O: no antigen, anti-A and anti-B, receives O only (universal donor)
formula_sheet.note: Rule: the donor's antigen must not meet the recipient's matching antibody.

formula_sheet.name: Rh and erythroblastosis foetalis
formula_sheet.expr: Rh antigen (rhesus monkey) in about 80 per cent of humans; Rh−ve mother with Rh+ve foetus, sensitised at first delivery, antibodies destroy RBCs of the second Rh+ve foetus
formula_sheet.note: Prevented by anti-Rh antibodies to the mother immediately after the first delivery.

formula_sheet.name: Coagulation cascade
formula_sheet.expr: Injury → platelet and tissue factors → thrombokinase; prothrombin → thrombin (by thrombokinase, needs Ca<sup>2+</sup>); fibrinogen → fibrin (by thrombin); fibrin network traps formed elements = clot
formula_sheet.note: Citrate, oxalate and EDTA prevent clotting by removing Ca<sup>2+</sup>; heparin is the natural anticoagulant.

formula_sheet.name: Vertebrate hearts
formula_sheet.expr: Fishes 2 chambers, single circulation; amphibians and reptiles (except crocodiles) 3 chambers, incomplete double circulation; crocodiles, birds, mammals 4 chambers, double circulation
formula_sheet.note: Open circulation: arthropods, molluscs. Closed: annelids, chordates.

formula_sheet.name: Heart location and valves
formula_sheet.expr: Thoracic cavity between the two lungs, tilted slightly left, mesodermal, size of a clenched fist, in the pericardium; tricuspid (right AV), bicuspid or mitral (left AV), semilunar (pulmonary artery and aorta)
formula_sheet.note: All valves permit one-way flow only. Left ventricle has the thickest wall.

formula_sheet.name: Conducting system
formula_sheet.expr: SAN (right upper corner of right atrium, 70 to 75 impulses per min, pacemaker) → AVN (lower left corner of right atrium near AV septum) → AV bundle (bundle of His) → right and left bundle branches → Purkinje fibres
formula_sheet.note: Nodal tissue is autoexcitable, so the heart is myogenic.

formula_sheet.name: Cardiac cycle numbers
formula_sheet.expr: Heart rate 72 per min; one cycle 0.8 s; atrial systole raises ventricular filling by about 30 per cent; stroke volume 70 mL; cardiac output = 70 × 72 ≈ 5000 mL per min
formula_sheet.note: Lub = closure of tricuspid and bicuspid valves; dub = closure of semilunar valves.

formula_sheet.name: ECG waves
formula_sheet.expr: P = atrial depolarisation; QRS = ventricular depolarisation (systole begins just after Q); T = ventricular repolarisation (end of T = end of systole)
formula_sheet.note: Three leads: one to each wrist and one to the left ankle. Count QRS complexes to get heart rate.

formula_sheet.name: Regulation of the heart
formula_sheet.expr: Medulla oblongata via ANS: sympathetic increases rate, force of ventricular contraction and cardiac output; parasympathetic decreases rate, conduction speed and cardiac output; adrenal medullary hormones increase cardiac output
formula_sheet.note: Basic rhythm is intrinsic (nodal tissue); nerves and hormones only modify it.

formula_sheet.name: Disorders
formula_sheet.expr: Normal BP 120/80 mm Hg; hypertension 140/90 or higher on repeated checks; CAD = deposits of calcium, fat, cholesterol, fibrous tissue in coronary arteries; angina = chest pain from too little O<sub>2</sub> to heart muscle; heart failure = ineffective pumping (congestive when lungs congest)
formula_sheet.note: Heart failure ≠ cardiac arrest (heart stops) ≠ heart attack (muscle damaged by inadequate blood supply).

diagrams.title: Formed elements of blood (NCERT Fig. 15.1)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a row of cells at the same scale. RBCs as biconcave discs (draw one face-on as a circle with a lighter centre and one edge-on as a dumbbell) with no nucleus. Then the five leucocytes, each with a nucleus: neutrophil with a multi-lobed nucleus and fine granules, eosinophil with a bilobed nucleus and coarse granules, basophil with an S-shaped nucleus hidden by dark granules, lymphocyte as a small cell with a large round nucleus filling it, monocyte as the largest cell with a kidney-shaped nucleus. End with platelets as tiny irregular fragments. Labels: erythrocyte (biconcave, no nucleus), neutrophil, eosinophil, basophil, lymphocyte, monocyte, platelets; group the first three as granulocytes and the next two as agranulocytes.

diagrams.title: Section of the human heart (NCERT Fig. 15.2)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw the heart as a rounded outline with the apex pointing down and to the viewer's right (the patient's left). Divide it by a vertical septum into left and right halves and by a horizontal line into upper atria and lower ventricles; draw the interventricular septum thick and the left ventricular wall thickest. Show the superior and inferior venae cavae entering the right atrium, the pulmonary artery leaving the right ventricle and branching, four pulmonary veins entering the left atrium, and the aorta arching up from the left ventricle. Draw the tricuspid valve as three flaps between right atrium and ventricle, the bicuspid as two flaps on the left, and small cup-shaped semilunar valves at the base of the pulmonary artery and aorta. Labels the scheme looks for: right atrium, left atrium, right ventricle, left ventricle, inter-atrial septum, inter-ventricular septum, tricuspid valve, bicuspid (mitral) valve, semilunar valves, superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, pulmonary artery, pulmonary veins, aorta. Optionally mark SAN and AVN in the right atrium.

diagrams.title: Conducting system (nodal tissue) of the heart
diagrams.how_to_draw: Use the same heart outline but show only the electrical pathway. Put a small oval marked SAN in the right upper corner of the right atrium near the superior vena cava, and a second oval marked AVN in the lower left corner of the right atrium next to the atrio-ventricular septum. From the AVN draw a thick line, the bundle of His, running down the top of the inter-ventricular septum and splitting into right and left bundle branches, each fanning out into fine Purkinje fibres through the ventricular walls. Add arrows for the direction of the impulse and write the sequence beside it: SAN → atria → AVN → bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibres → ventricles. Labels: SAN (pacemaker), AVN, AV bundle (bundle of His), right and left bundle branches, Purkinje fibres.

diagrams.title: Cardiac cycle in three stages (NCERT Fig. 15.3)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw three simplified hearts side by side. (a) Joint diastole: all four chambers relaxed, tricuspid and bicuspid drawn open with arrows from the venae cavae and pulmonary veins passing through the atria into the ventricles, semilunar valves closed. (b) Atrial systole: atria drawn contracted (smaller), arrows pushing blood into the ventricles, AV valves open, semilunar closed. (c) Ventricular systole: ventricles drawn contracted, AV valves closed, semilunar valves open with arrows into the pulmonary artery and aorta, atria relaxed and filling. Label each stage with its name and its valve state, and add 'lub' under (c) at the AV closure and 'dub' at the start of the next diastole when the semilunar valves close. State total duration 0.8 s.

diagrams.title: Standard electrocardiogram (NCERT Fig. 15.4)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a horizontal baseline (time on the x-axis, voltage on the y-axis). From left: a small rounded upward bump labelled P, a flat segment, a sharp small downward dip Q, a tall narrow upward spike R, a small downward dip S back to baseline, a flat S-T segment, then a broader rounded upward hump T, then baseline until the next P. Label P, Q, R, S, T; bracket QRS as the QRS complex. Write beside them: P = atrial depolarisation, QRS = ventricular depolarisation (systole begins after Q), T = ventricular repolarisation (end of T = end of systole). Optionally mark the P-Q interval and the S-T segment.

diagrams.title: Schematic plan of blood circulation in humans (NCERT Fig. 15.5)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw the heart as a box divided into four cells labelled RA, RV, LA, LV, with a box for the lungs above it and a box for the body tissues below. Arrows: body → venae cavae → RA → RV → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → LA → LV → aorta → body. Shade the right side and pulmonary artery blue for deoxygenated blood and the left side and pulmonary veins red for oxygenated blood. Label the upper loop 'pulmonary circulation' and the lower loop 'systemic circulation'. Add a side branch from the intestine to the liver labelled hepatic portal vein and a small loop labelled coronary circulation. Labels: right and left atrium, right and left ventricle, pulmonary artery, pulmonary veins, aorta, superior and inferior vena cava, lungs, body tissues, hepatic portal system.

diagrams.title: Flow chart of blood coagulation
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a vertical flow chart with boxes and arrows. Top: injury to tissue or blood vessel. Two arrows down: 'platelets release factors' and 'damaged tissue releases factors'. These join into a box 'cascade of inactive plasma factors activated'. Arrow down to 'thrombokinase (enzyme complex)'. Draw a side-by-side pair: prothrombin (inactive) → thrombin (active), with thrombokinase and Ca<sup>2+</sup> written on the arrow. Then fibrinogen (soluble) → fibrin (insoluble threads), with thrombin on the arrow. Bottom box: fibrin network traps dead and damaged formed elements → clot (coagulum). Label every enzyme and mark the two places Ca<sup>2+</sup> is required.

diagrams.title: Evolution of the vertebrate heart (2-, 3- and 4-chambered)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw three simple heart diagrams in a row. Fish: two chambers stacked, one atrium above one ventricle, single arrow path: body → atrium → ventricle → gills → body; label 'single circulation, deoxygenated blood only through the heart'. Amphibian or reptile: two atria over one ventricle; colour the left atrium red (from lungs or skin), the right atrium blue (from body) and the ventricle purple to show mixing; label 'incomplete double circulation'. Bird or mammal: two atria over two ventricles with a complete septum; right side blue, left side red; label 'double circulation, no mixing'. Under each write the examples: fishes; amphibians and reptiles except crocodiles; crocodiles, birds and mammals.

diagrams.title: Open versus closed circulatory system
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw two schematic animals. Left, an insect or a mollusc: a tubular heart pumping into a short vessel that opens into large shaded spaces (sinuses or haemocoel) around the organs, with blood returning to the heart through openings; label 'open circulation: blood in sinuses, organs bathed directly, low pressure, less precise regulation; arthropods and molluscs'. Right, an earthworm or a mammal: a heart connected to a continuous loop of arteries, capillaries and veins with no gaps; label 'closed circulation: blood always within vessels, high pressure, flow precisely regulated; annelids and chordates'.

ncert_questions.q: Name the components of the formed elements in the blood and mention one major function of each of them.
ncert_questions.a:
The formed elements are erythrocytes, leucocytes and platelets, about 45 per cent of blood.

  • Erythrocytes (RBCs): transport of respiratory gases, O2 and CO2, through haemoglobin.
  • Leucocytes (WBCs): defence of the body. Neutrophils and monocytes are phagocytic and destroy foreign organisms; basophils secrete histamine, serotonin and heparin and are involved in inflammatory reactions; eosinophils resist infections and are associated with allergic reactions; lymphocytes (B and T) are responsible for immune responses.
  • Platelets (thrombocytes): release substances involved in the coagulation of blood.

ncert_questions.q: What is the importance of plasma proteins?
ncert_questions.a:
Plasma contains 6 to 8 per cent proteins, of three main kinds, each with a specific role.

  • Fibrinogen is needed for clotting or coagulation of blood; thrombin converts it into fibrin threads that form the clot.
  • Globulins are involved primarily in the defence mechanisms of the body; the gamma globulins are the antibodies.
  • Albumins help in osmotic balance; they hold water in the blood vessels and maintain blood volume and pressure.

Plasma proteins also help maintain the pH of blood by acting as buffers, and some, such as prothrombin, are inactive factors of the clotting cascade.

ncert_questions.q: Match Column I with Column II: (a) Eosinophils, (b) RBC, (c) AB group, (d) Platelets, (e) Systole; with (i) Coagulation, (ii) Universal recipient, (iii) Resist infections, (iv) Contraction of heart, (v) Gas transport.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Eosinophils – (iii) Resist infections
(b) RBC – (v) Gas transport
(c) AB group – (ii) Universal recipient
(d) Platelets – (i) Coagulation
(e) Systole – (iv) Contraction of heart

ncert_questions.q: Why do we consider blood as a connective tissue?
ncert_questions.a: Blood is considered a connective tissue because it has all the features of one: (i) it is mesodermal in origin, like other connective tissues; (ii) it consists of cells (the formed elements) scattered in a non-living matrix (plasma); the matrix is fluid and fibres appear only as fibrin during clotting; (iii) it connects different parts of the body by transporting gases, nutrients, hormones and wastes between them. NCERT therefore calls it a special connective tissue with a fluid matrix.

ncert_questions.q: What is the difference between lymph and blood?
ncert_questions.a:
• Colour: blood is red due to haemoglobin in RBCs; lymph is colourless because it has no RBCs.
  • Cells: blood has RBCs, all types of WBCs and platelets; lymph has only leucocytes, mainly lymphocytes, and no platelets.
  • Proteins: blood plasma has more proteins including fibrinogen; lymph has fewer proteins and clots slowly.
  • Flow: blood flows in a closed circuit from the heart and back; lymph flows in one direction only, from the tissues to the veins.
  • Function: blood transports O2, CO2, nutrients and wastes; lymph returns tissue fluid to blood, carries absorbed fats from the lacteals and provides immunity.

ncert_questions.q: What is meant by double circulation? What is its significance?
ncert_questions.a:
Double circulation is the pattern in which blood passes through the heart twice in one complete circuit of the body. The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary artery to the lungs, and oxygenated blood returns by the pulmonary veins to the left atrium: the pulmonary circulation. The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood through the aorta to the body tissues, and deoxygenated blood returns through the venae cavae to the right atrium: the systemic circulation. It is found in birds and mammals.

Significance: oxygenated and deoxygenated blood are kept completely separate, so the tissues receive fully oxygenated blood; the left ventricle can send blood to the body at high pressure while the lungs receive it at a gentler pressure; the efficient supply of O2 supports the high metabolic rate and constant body temperature of birds and mammals.

ncert_questions.q: Write the differences between blood and lymph, and between open and closed systems of circulation.
ncert_questions.a:
Blood versus lymph: blood is red (haemoglobin), has RBCs, WBCs and platelets, more plasma proteins, flows in a closed circuit and transports gases, nutrients and wastes; lymph is colourless, has only lymphocytes, fewer proteins, flows one way from tissues to veins, and carries absorbed fats and lymphocytes for immunity.

Open versus closed circulation: in the open system (arthropods, molluscs) blood pumped by the heart passes through large vessels into open sinuses and bathes the organs directly, at low pressure, with little control over its distribution; in the closed system (annelids, chordates) blood always stays inside a closed network of vessels, flows at higher pressure and speed, and its flow to different organs can be precisely regulated, which is why it is considered more advantageous.

ncert_questions.q: Write the differences between systole and diastole, and between the P-wave and the T-wave.
ncert_questions.a:
Systole versus diastole: systole is the contraction phase of a heart chamber, during which pressure rises and blood is pushed out (atrial systole into the ventricles, ventricular systole into the pulmonary artery and aorta); diastole is the relaxation phase, during which pressure falls and the chamber fills with blood. In one 0.8 s cycle, ventricular systole lasts about 0.3 s and ventricular diastole about 0.5 s.

P-wave versus T-wave: the P-wave is the small first wave of the ECG and represents the depolarisation (electrical excitation) of the atria, leading to atrial contraction; the T-wave is the last wave and represents the repolarisation of the ventricles, their return from the excited to the normal state, and its end marks the end of systole.

ncert_questions.q: Describe the evolutionary change in the pattern of heart among the vertebrates.
ncert_questions.a:
All vertebrates have a muscular chambered heart, but the number of chambers increases along the evolutionary series, and with it the separation of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.

  1. Fishes: a two-chambered heart with one atrium and one ventricle. The heart pumps deoxygenated blood to the gills for oxygenation; from the gills it goes to the body and returns deoxygenated. Blood passes through the heart once per circuit: single circulation.
  2. Amphibians and reptiles (except crocodiles): a three-chambered heart with two atria and one ventricle. The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the gills, lungs or skin and the right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the body, but both empty into the single ventricle, where the blood mixes and is pumped out as mixed blood: incomplete double circulation.
  3. Crocodiles, birds and mammals: a four-chambered heart with two atria and two ventricles. Oxygenated blood in the left atrium goes to the left ventricle and deoxygenated blood in the right atrium goes to the right ventricle; the ventricles pump without mixing, giving two separate circuits, pulmonary and systemic: complete double circulation.

The trend is towards complete separation of the two kinds of blood, which allows efficient oxygen delivery and the high metabolic rate of endothermic birds and mammals.

ncert_questions.q: Why do we call our heart myogenic?
ncert_questions.a: The normal activities of the human heart are regulated intrinsically, that is, auto-regulated by specialised cardiac muscle called the nodal tissue, which is autoexcitable and can generate action potentials without any external (nervous) stimulus. The sino-atrial node generates the impulse that initiates and maintains each heart beat, and it is conducted through the AVN, the bundle of His and the Purkinje fibres, all of which are muscle, not nerve. Because the beat originates in the heart muscle itself, the heart is called myogenic. Nerves of the autonomic nervous system only modify the rate, which is why a heart removed from the body or a transplanted heart continues to beat.

ncert_questions.q: Sino-atrial node is called the pacemaker of our heart. Why?
ncert_questions.a: The sino-atrial node (SAN) is a patch of nodal tissue in the right upper corner of the right atrium. All nodal tissue is autoexcitable, but the number of action potentials that can be generated per minute varies at different parts of the nodal system, and the SAN generates the maximum, 70 to 75 per minute. Because it fires fastest, it sets the rhythm for the whole heart, and it is therefore responsible for initiating and maintaining the rhythmic contractile activity of the heart. A structure that sets the pace of the beat is a pacemaker, so the SAN is called the pacemaker of the heart.

ncert_questions.q: What is the significance of atrio-ventricular node and atrio-ventricular bundle in the functioning of heart?
ncert_questions.a: The atrio-ventricular node (AVN) lies in the lower left corner of the right atrium close to the atrio-ventricular septum. It receives the impulse generated by the SAN after it has spread over the atria, and transmits it to the ventricles; since the atria and ventricles are separated by the fibrous atrio-ventricular septum, the AVN is the only electrical route between them. It also delays the impulse slightly, so the atria finish contracting and emptying before the ventricles begin. The atrio-ventricular bundle (bundle of His) continues from the AVN, passes through the atrio-ventricular septa, emerges on top of the inter-ventricular septum and divides into right and left bundles, which give rise to the Purkinje fibres in the ventricular musculature. Together they conduct the impulse rapidly to all parts of both ventricles so that the ventricles contract simultaneously and forcefully from the apex upward, pushing blood into the pulmonary artery and the aorta.

ncert_questions.q: Define a cardiac cycle and the cardiac output.
ncert_questions.a:
Cardiac cycle: the sequential events in the heart that are cyclically repeated, consisting of the systole (contraction) and diastole (relaxation) of both the atria and the ventricles, together with the opening and closing of the valves. It begins with joint diastole, followed by atrial systole, ventricular systole and ventricular diastole. The heart beats 72 times per minute, so one cardiac cycle lasts about 0.8 s.

Cardiac output: the volume of blood pumped out by each ventricle per minute. It equals the stroke volume (about 70 mL per beat) multiplied by the heart rate (72 per minute): 70 × 72 = 5040 mL, about 5000 mL or 5 litres per minute in a normal adult. The body can alter the stroke volume and the heart rate and hence the cardiac output; an athlete's cardiac output is much higher.

During each cardiac cycle two prominent sounds are produced, which can be heard through a stethoscope. The first heart sound, lub, is associated with the closure of the tricuspid and bicuspid (atrio-ventricular) valves at the beginning of ventricular systole, when the rising ventricular pressure attempts to push blood back into the atria. It is longer and lower-pitched. The second heart sound, dub, is associated with the closure of the semilunar valves at the beginning of ventricular diastole, when the falling ventricular pressure would let blood flow back from the aorta and the pulmonary artery. It is shorter and sharper. The sounds are of clinical diagnostic significance: an abnormal sound or murmur indicates a defective valve.

ncert_questions.q: Draw a standard ECG and explain the different segments in it.
ncert_questions.a:
[Draw the ECG as in the diagram section: baseline, small P bump, sharp Q dip, tall R spike, S dip, flat segment, broad T hump; label P, Q, R, S, T and the QRS complex.]

An electrocardiogram is a graphical representation of the electrical activity of the heart during a cardiac cycle, obtained by connecting the patient to an electrocardiograph with three electrical leads, one to each wrist and one to the left ankle.

  • P wave: the electrical excitation (depolarisation) of the atria, which leads to contraction of both atria.
  • QRS complex: the depolarisation of the ventricles, which initiates ventricular contraction; the contraction starts shortly after Q and marks the beginning of systole.
  • T wave: the return of the ventricles from the excited to the normal state (repolarisation); the end of the T wave marks the end of systole.

Since ECGs from different individuals have roughly the same shape for a given lead configuration, any deviation indicates a possible abnormality or disease, so the ECG has great clinical significance. Counting the number of QRS complexes in a given time gives the heart beat rate.

pyq.q: Which of the following leucocytes does not show phagocytic activity?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Basophils secrete histamine, serotonin and heparin and take part in inflammatory reactions; they are not phagocytic. Neutrophils, monocytes and the macrophages derived from monocytes are phagocytic.

pyq.q: Serum differs from blood in
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Serum is plasma from which the clotting factors, mainly fibrinogen, have been removed. Albumins, globulins and antibodies remain in it.

pyq.q: Adult human RBCs are enucleate. Which of the following is the most appropriate explanation for this feature?
options: They do not need to reproduce
All their internal space is available for oxygen transport
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: The lost nucleus and organelles leave the entire volume of the biconcave cell packed with haemoglobin for gas transport. RBCs still metabolise (anaerobically), so option c is wrong.

pyq.q: A person with blood group AB is called a universal recipient because
options: His RBCs have neither antigen A nor B
His plasma has both anti-A and anti-B antibodies
His plasma has no anti-A or anti-B antibodies
His RBCs have the Rh antigen
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: AB RBCs carry both antigens A and B, so the plasma has no antibodies against either; donor RBCs of any ABO group are therefore not agglutinated.

pyq.q: The correct sequence of conduction of the cardiac impulse is
options: SAN → AVN → Purkinje fibres → bundle of His
SAN → AVN → bundle of His → Purkinje fibres
AVN → SAN → bundle of His → Purkinje fibres
SAN → bundle of His → AVN → Purkinje fibres
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: The impulse starts in the SAN, spreads over the atria to the AVN, passes down the AV bundle (bundle of His) and its branches, and reaches the ventricular muscle through the Purkinje fibres.

pyq.q: In the ECG, the QRS complex represents
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: P is atrial depolarisation, QRS is ventricular depolarisation and T is ventricular repolarisation. Atrial repolarisation is masked by the QRS complex.

pyq.q: Which of the following animals has a three-chambered heart?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Amphibians and reptiles except crocodiles have two atria and one ventricle. Crocodiles and birds have four chambers; the shark, a fish, has two.

pyq.q: Stroke volume is 70 mL and heart rate is 75 per minute. The cardiac output is
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate = 70 × 75 = 5250 mL per minute. The textbook value of 5000 mL uses 72 beats per minute.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The human heart is called myogenic. Reason (R): The rhythm of the heart beat is initiated by the nodal tissue, which is autoexcitable, and not by nerves.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Myogenic means the beat originates in the heart muscle; the autoexcitable nodal tissue (SAN) is exactly that muscle, so R explains A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Erythroblastosis foetalis usually affects the second Rh-positive child of an Rh-negative mother, not the first. Reason (R): The mother forms anti-Rh antibodies only after exposure to foetal Rh-positive blood during the delivery of the first child.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: During the first pregnancy the placenta keeps the two bloods apart; sensitisation occurs at the first delivery, and the antibodies formed then cross the placenta in the next pregnancy. R is the correct explanation.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The first heart sound (lub) is produced at the beginning of ventricular systole. Reason (R): The first heart sound is due to the closure of the semilunar valves.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Lub is heard at the start of ventricular systole, but it is caused by closure of the tricuspid and bicuspid (AV) valves. The semilunar valves closing gives the second sound, dub, so R is false.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Blood group O is called the universal donor. Reason (R): The plasma of blood group O has no antibodies.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: O is the universal donor because its RBCs have no antigen A or B. Its plasma actually contains both anti-A and anti-B antibodies, so R is false.

pyq.q: Distinguish between plasma and serum.
pyq.answer: Plasma is the straw-coloured fluid matrix of blood obtained when the formed elements are separated from unclotted blood; it contains all the plasma proteins including fibrinogen and the other clotting factors in inactive form. Serum is the fluid that separates from blood after it has clotted; it is plasma minus the clotting factors, so it has no fibrinogen but retains albumins, globulins (antibodies), minerals and nutrients. Plasma can clot; serum cannot.

pyq.q: Name the two categories of leucocytes and the cells in each. Which is the most abundant and which the least abundant leucocyte?
pyq.answer: Granulocytes: neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils. Agranulocytes: lymphocytes and monocytes. The most abundant leucocyte is the neutrophil (60 to 65 per cent of WBCs) and the least abundant is the basophil (0.5 to 1 per cent).

pyq.q: Why is blood group O called the universal donor and blood group AB the universal recipient?
pyq.answer: Group O RBCs carry no antigen A or B, so they are not agglutinated by the anti-A or anti-B antibodies of any recipient; O blood can therefore be given to A, B, AB and O, making O the universal donor. Group AB plasma has no anti-A or anti-B antibodies, so RBCs of any ABO group given to an AB person are not agglutinated; AB can receive from A, B, AB and O, making AB the universal recipient.

pyq.q: State the location and the role of the sino-atrial node and the atrio-ventricular node.
pyq.answer: The SAN lies in the right upper corner of the right atrium; it generates the maximum number of action potentials (70 to 75 per minute) and initiates and maintains the rhythm of the heart beat, acting as the pacemaker. The AVN lies in the lower left corner of the right atrium close to the atrio-ventricular septum; it receives the impulse from the atria and passes it on through the AV bundle to the ventricles, so it is the only electrical link between atria and ventricles.

pyq.q: Name the animals with (i) an open circulatory system and (ii) a closed circulatory system. Which is more advantageous and why?
pyq.answer: (i) Open circulatory system: arthropods and molluscs; blood flows from the heart into open sinuses. (ii) Closed circulatory system: annelids and chordates; blood always flows within a closed network of vessels. The closed system is more advantageous because the flow of blood can be more precisely regulated, directed to the organs that need it at a controlled pressure and speed.

pyq.q: What is the difference between cardiac arrest, heart attack and heart failure?
pyq.answer: Heart failure is the state in which the heart is not pumping blood effectively enough to meet the needs of the body (called congestive heart failure when congestion of the lungs is a main symptom). Cardiac arrest is when the heart stops beating altogether. Heart attack is when the heart muscle is suddenly damaged by an inadequate blood supply, usually from a blocked coronary artery.

pyq.q: Describe the mechanism of blood coagulation.
pyq.answer:
Coagulation is the response of blood to injury that prevents excessive loss of blood. It is a cascade of linked enzymic reactions involving factors present in the plasma in an inactive state.

  1. Injury to a tissue stimulates the platelets to release certain factors, and the damaged tissues also release factors; these activate the inactive plasma factors one after another, producing the enzyme complex thrombokinase.
  2. Thrombokinase, in the presence of Ca2+, converts the inactive plasma protein prothrombin into the active enzyme thrombin.
  3. Thrombin converts the soluble plasma protein fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads.

The network of fibrin threads traps dead and damaged formed elements of blood and forms the clot or coagulum, a dark reddish brown scum at the site of injury. Calcium ions play a very important role in clotting; removing them (with citrate or oxalate) prevents it.

pyq.q: What is erythroblastosis foetalis? How can it be prevented?
pyq.answer:
Erythroblastosis foetalis is a special case of Rh incompatibility between an Rh-negative mother and an Rh-positive foetus. During the first pregnancy the Rh antigens of the foetus are not exposed to the mother's blood because the placenta separates the two bloods. During the delivery of the first child, however, small amounts of the foetal Rh-positive blood may enter the maternal blood, and the mother starts producing anti-Rh antibodies. In a subsequent pregnancy with an Rh-positive foetus, these antibodies leak across the placenta into the foetal blood and destroy the foetal RBCs, causing severe anaemia and jaundice in the baby; the condition can be fatal.

Prevention: anti-Rh antibodies are administered to the mother immediately after the delivery of the first child. They destroy any foetal Rh-positive RBCs in her circulation before her immune system is sensitised, so no antibodies of her own are formed and the next pregnancy is safe.

pyq.q: Explain the three stages of the cardiac cycle with the state of the valves in each.
pyq.answer:
1. Joint diastole: all four chambers are relaxed. The tricuspid and bicuspid valves are open, so blood from the venae cavae and pulmonary veins flows through the right and left atria into the ventricles; the semilunar valves are closed.
  2. Atrial systole: the SAN fires and both atria contract together, increasing the flow of blood into the ventricles by about 30 per cent. AV valves remain open, semilunar valves closed.
  3. Ventricular systole: the impulse reaches the ventricles through the AVN, AV bundle and Purkinje fibres, and both ventricles contract while the atria relax. The rising ventricular pressure closes the tricuspid and bicuspid valves (first sound, lub) and then forces the semilunar valves open, so blood enters the pulmonary artery and the aorta. As the ventricles relax (ventricular diastole), the falling pressure closes the semilunar valves (second sound, dub), and when it falls further the AV valves reopen and the cycle returns to joint diastole.

The whole cycle takes about 0.8 s at 72 beats per minute; each ventricle pumps a stroke volume of about 70 mL, giving a cardiac output of about 5 L per minute.

pyq.q: How is the activity of the heart regulated by the nervous system and by hormones?
pyq.answer:
