The basic rhythm of the heart is set intrinsically by the autoexcitable nodal tissue (the SAN), which is why the heart is myogenic. This rhythm is moderated by a special neural centre in the medulla oblongata acting through the autonomic nervous system.

  • Sympathetic nerves increase the rate of heart beat, the strength of ventricular contraction and thereby the cardiac output (as in exercise or fear).
  • Parasympathetic nerves (vagus) decrease the rate of heart beat, the speed of conduction of the action potential and thereby the cardiac output (as at rest).
  • Adrenal medullary hormones, adrenaline and noradrenaline, also increase the cardiac output.

pyq.q: Explain the ABO blood grouping with reference to antigens and antibodies, and state which groups a person of group B can safely receive blood from.
pyq.answer:
ABO grouping is based on the presence or absence of two surface antigens, A and B, on the RBCs, and of two natural antibodies, anti-A and anti-B, in the plasma. Group A has antigen A and antibody anti-B; group B has antigen B and antibody anti-A; group AB has both antigens and no antibodies; group O has no antigens and both antibodies. Transfusion is safe only when the donor's RBC antigen does not meet the matching antibody in the recipient's plasma; otherwise the RBCs are agglutinated and destroyed.

A person of group B has anti-A antibodies, so any donor RBCs with antigen A (groups A and AB) would be agglutinated. He can safely receive blood from group B and group O (O has no antigen). The Rh group must also be matched.

pyq.q: Draw a labelled diagram of a section of the human heart and describe its chambers, septa and valves.
pyq.answer:
[Draw the heart as in the diagram section with right and left atria, right and left ventricles, inter-atrial and inter-ventricular septa, tricuspid, bicuspid and semilunar valves, superior and inferior venae cavae, pulmonary artery, pulmonary veins and aorta labelled.]

The human heart is mesodermally derived, lies in the thoracic cavity between the two lungs, slightly tilted to the left, is the size of a clenched fist and is enclosed in the double-walled pericardium containing pericardial fluid.

Chambers: two relatively small upper chambers, the atria, which receive blood (the right atrium from the venae cavae, the left from the pulmonary veins), and two larger lower chambers, the ventricles, which pump blood out (the right ventricle into the pulmonary artery, the left into the aorta). The ventricular walls are much thicker than the atrial walls, and the left ventricular wall is the thickest because it pumps to the whole body.

Septa: a thin muscular inter-atrial septum separates the two atria; a thick inter-ventricular septum separates the two ventricles; a thick fibrous atrio-ventricular septum separates the atrium and ventricle of each side, with one opening on each side.

Valves: the right atrio-ventricular opening is guarded by the tricuspid valve (three cusps) and the left by the bicuspid or mitral valve (two cusps); the openings of the right and left ventricles into the pulmonary artery and the aorta are guarded by semilunar valves. All valves allow blood to flow in one direction only, from atria to ventricles and from ventricles to the arteries, and prevent backflow. The heart wall is cardiac muscle, and the nodal tissue (SAN, AVN, bundle of His, Purkinje fibres) within it generates and conducts the impulse.

pyq.q: Explain double circulation in humans with a schematic diagram. Mention the hepatic portal system and the coronary circulation. Why is double circulation significant?
pyq.answer:
[Draw the schematic plan: heart as four boxes RA, RV, LA, LV; lungs above; body tissues below; arrows body → venae cavae → RA → RV → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → LA → LV → aorta → body; upper loop labelled pulmonary circulation, lower loop systemic circulation.]

Pulmonary circulation: deoxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium through the superior and inferior venae cavae, passes through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle, and is pumped through the pulmonary artery to the lungs, where it is oxygenated. The pulmonary veins carry the oxygenated blood back to the left atrium.

Systemic circulation: from the left atrium blood passes through the bicuspid valve to the left ventricle, which pumps it into the aorta. A network of arteries, arterioles and capillaries carries it to the tissues, supplying nutrients, O2 and other essential substances and collecting CO2 and other harmful substances; venules, veins and the venae cavae return the deoxygenated blood to the right atrium.

Because blood passes through the heart twice in one complete circuit, the pattern is called double circulation. Two special circuits: the hepatic portal system, in which the hepatic portal vein carries blood from the intestine to the liver before it joins the systemic circulation, and the coronary system of vessels exclusively supplying the cardiac musculature.

Significance: oxygenated and deoxygenated blood never mix, so tissues receive fully oxygenated blood; the body is supplied at high pressure by the thick-walled left ventricle while the lungs are supplied at low pressure; and the efficient O2 supply supports the high metabolic rate and constant body temperature of mammals and birds.

pyq.q: Describe blood as a tissue. Give the composition of plasma and the counts, structure and functions of the formed elements.
pyq.answer:
Blood is a special connective tissue consisting of a fluid matrix, plasma, and formed elements; it is mesodermal in origin and connects all parts of the body by transporting materials.

Plasma (55 per cent of blood) is a straw-coloured viscous fluid: 90 to 92 per cent water and 6 to 8 per cent proteins (fibrinogen for clotting, globulins for defence, albumins for osmotic balance), plus glucose, amino acids, lipids, minerals (Na+, Ca2+, Mg2+, HCO3−, Cl−) and inactive clotting factors. Plasma without clotting factors is serum.

Formed elements (45 per cent):

  • Erythrocytes: 5 to 5.5 million per mm3; biconcave, enucleate in most mammals, formed in red bone marrow; contain the iron-containing protein haemoglobin (12 to 16 g per 100 mL); transport respiratory gases; life span 120 days, destroyed in the spleen.
  • Leucocytes: 6000 to 8000 per mm3; colourless, nucleated, short-lived. Granulocytes: neutrophils (60 to 65 per cent, phagocytic), eosinophils (2 to 3 per cent, resist infection, allergy), basophils (0.5 to 1 per cent, secrete histamine, serotonin and heparin, inflammation). Agranulocytes: lymphocytes (20 to 25 per cent, B and T cells, immune responses), monocytes (6 to 8 per cent, phagocytic).
  • Platelets (thrombocytes): 1.5 to 3.5 lakh per mm3; cell fragments from megakaryocytes of the bone marrow; release substances involved in coagulation; their reduction leads to clotting disorders and excessive loss of blood.

pyq.q:
A 24-year-old woman with blood group O negative delivered a healthy Rh-positive baby two years ago. She is now pregnant again and her doctor has ordered a test for anti-Rh antibodies in her blood.
(i) Why is the second pregnancy a concern when the first baby was healthy?
(ii) Name the condition the second baby may develop and state two of its effects.
(iii) What should have been done immediately after the first delivery to prevent this?
(iv) If this woman ever needs a transfusion, from which ABO and Rh group can she receive blood?
pyq.answer:
(i) During the first pregnancy the placenta kept the foetal Rh-positive blood away from the mother's blood. At the first delivery some foetal blood entered her circulation, and being Rh-negative she began forming anti-Rh antibodies. In the second pregnancy these antibodies can cross the placenta and attack the RBCs of an Rh-positive foetus.
(ii) Erythroblastosis foetalis; the foetal RBCs are destroyed, causing severe anaemia and jaundice, and the condition can be fatal.
(iii) Anti-Rh antibodies should have been administered to the mother immediately after the first delivery, to destroy foetal Rh-positive cells before her immune system was sensitised.
(iv) Only group O, and only Rh-negative blood; her plasma has anti-A and anti-B antibodies, and she must not be exposed to the Rh antigen.

pyq.q:
A 5-second strip of a standard ECG recorded from a resting adult shows 6 complete P-QRS-T cycles. The doctor notes that the shape of every wave is normal.
(i) Calculate the heart rate of this person.
(ii) Which wave indicates the contraction of the atria, and what electrical event does it represent?
(iii) Between which two points of the trace does ventricular systole occur?
(iv) Why is the ECG useful for diagnosing heart disease? Name the leads used for a standard ECG.
pyq.answer:
(i) 6 cycles in 5 s means 6 QRS complexes in 5 s; heart rate = 6 × (60 ÷ 5) = 72 beats per minute, a normal resting rate.
(ii) The P wave; it represents the depolarisation (electrical excitation) of the atria, which leads to atrial contraction.
(iii) Ventricular systole begins shortly after the Q wave (the QRS complex is ventricular depolarisation) and ends at the end of the T wave (ventricular repolarisation).
(iv) ECGs of different individuals have roughly the same shape for a given lead configuration, so any deviation from the normal shape indicates a possible abnormality or disease of the heart. A standard ECG uses three electrical leads, one to each wrist and one to the left ankle.

common_mistakes: Swapping basophils and eosinophils. Basophils secrete histamine, serotonin and heparin (inflammation); eosinophils resist infection and are linked to allergy. Neutrophils and monocytes are the phagocytes. The examiner deducts the whole mark for a swap.

Mixing up the counts. RBCs 5 to 5.5 million, WBCs 6000 to 8000, platelets 1.5 to 3.5 lakh, all per mm<sup>3</sup>; haemoglobin 12 to 16 g per 100 mL. Writing 'per mL' or dropping the unit costs the mark in a 1-mark question.

Getting the enzyme sequence of clotting wrong. Thrombokinase converts prothrombin to thrombin; thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin. Students often write 'thrombokinase converts fibrinogen' or forget Ca<sup>2+</sup>.

Writing that group O is the universal donor because it has no antibodies. O has no antigens on its RBCs but has both antibodies in plasma. AB is the universal recipient because it has no antibodies. The reasoning is the marking point, not just the group name.

In erythroblastosis foetalis, writing that the first child is affected or that the mother is Rh-positive. It is the Rh-negative mother, the Rh-positive foetus, and a subsequent pregnancy; prevention is anti-Rh antibodies to the mother immediately after the first delivery.

Placing the nodes wrongly. Both the SAN (right upper corner) and the AVN (lower left corner, near the AV septum) lie in the right atrium. Drawing the AVN in the ventricle or the SAN in the left atrium loses the label marks.

Reversing the heart sounds. Lub is the closure of the tricuspid and bicuspid valves at the start of ventricular systole; dub is the closure of the semilunar valves at the start of ventricular diastole.

Writing 'contraction' and 'relaxation' for the ECG waves instead of depolarisation and repolarisation, or saying the T wave is atrial repolarisation. P is atrial depolarisation, QRS ventricular depolarisation, T ventricular repolarisation.

Calling the pulmonary artery an oxygenated vessel. It is the only artery carrying deoxygenated blood; the pulmonary veins are the only veins carrying oxygenated blood. Colouring them the wrong way in the schematic diagram is penalised.
Treating heart failure, cardiac arrest and heart attack as synonyms, or saying 'all reptiles have three-chambered hearts' without the crocodile exception.
strategy:
This is a fact-dense chapter and the school paper tests recall of the exact NCERT numbers and names more than reasoning, so build a one-page fact sheet first: the composition of plasma, the three counts and the five leucocyte percentages, the ABO table, the clotting cascade with its two enzymes, the positions of the SAN and AVN, 0.8 s, 70 mL, 72 per minute, 5 L, the three ECG waves, 120/80 and 140/90. Say them aloud until you can write the sheet from memory in ten minutes.

Spend the next block on the four diagrams that appear in long questions: the section of the heart, the ECG, the schematic plan of circulation and the formed elements. Draw each twice without looking, then check every label against the figure in NCERT. A heart diagram with all fourteen labels is worth as much as a full page of writing.

Then work through the NCERT exercise questions in order; questions 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 and 14 have appeared almost verbatim in school papers for years. Write the answers in the format above, with bold key terms and numbered steps for the cardiac cycle, the coagulation cascade and the evolution of the heart.

Finally, practise the three differences the examiner loves, blood versus lymph, open versus closed circulation, and systole versus diastole, as tables with three or four points each, and be able to give the one-line definitions of hypertension, CAD, angina and heart failure and the difference between heart failure, cardiac arrest and heart attack. In the exam, answer the diagram-based long question first while your memory of the labels is fresh, and keep 1-mark answers to one precise sentence with the number or name the question wants.
revision_checklist: Plasma is 55 per cent of blood, 90 to 92 per cent water, 6 to 8 per cent proteins: fibrinogen (clotting), globulins (defence), albumins (osmotic balance); serum = plasma minus clotting factors.
RBCs: 5 to 5.5 million per mm<sup>3</sup>, biconcave, enucleate, red bone marrow, haemoglobin 12 to 16 g per 100 mL, 120 days, destroyed in spleen.

WBCs: 6000 to 8000 per mm<sup>3</sup>; neutrophils 60 to 65 per cent (phagocytic), lymphocytes 20 to 25 (B and T, immunity), monocytes 6 to 8 (phagocytic), eosinophils 2 to 3 (allergy), basophils 0.5 to 1 (histamine, serotonin, heparin).
Platelets: 1.5 to 3.5 lakh per mm<sup>3</sup>, from megakaryocytes, release clotting factors.
ABO table: antigen on RBC, antibody in plasma, safe donors; O universal donor (no antigen), AB universal recipient (no antibody).
Rh antigen (rhesus monkey, 80 per cent of humans); erythroblastosis foetalis: Rh−ve mother, Rh+ve foetus, second pregnancy, anaemia and jaundice; anti-Rh antibodies after first delivery prevent it.
Clotting: platelet and tissue factors → thrombokinase; prothrombin → thrombin (Ca<sup>2+</sup>); fibrinogen → fibrin; fibrin network traps formed elements.
Lymph: colourless, lymphocytes, no RBCs or platelets, carries fats from lacteals; blood versus lymph differences.
Open circulation: arthropods, molluscs (sinuses); closed: annelids, chordates (vessels, precise regulation).
Hearts: fishes 2 chambers single circulation; amphibians and reptiles except crocodiles 3 chambers incomplete double; crocodiles, birds, mammals 4 chambers double circulation.

Human heart: thoracic cavity between lungs, tilted left, pericardium; inter-atrial, inter-ventricular and AV septa; tricuspid (right), bicuspid or mitral (left), semilunar (pulmonary artery and aorta); can draw and label Fig. 15.2.
Nodal tissue: SAN right upper corner of right atrium (pacemaker, 70 to 75 per min) → AVN lower left corner of right atrium → bundle of His → branches → Purkinje fibres; autoexcitable, so myogenic.

Cardiac cycle: joint diastole → atrial systole (+30 per cent filling) → ventricular systole → ventricular diastole; 0.8 s; stroke volume 70 mL; cardiac output 5 L per min; lub = AV valves close, dub = semilunar valves close.
ECG: three leads (wrists and left ankle); P atrial depolarisation, QRS ventricular depolarisation, T ventricular repolarisation; count QRS for heart rate.
Double circulation: pulmonary (RV → lungs → LA) and systemic (LV → body → RA); hepatic portal system; coronary system; significance.
Regulation: medulla oblongata via ANS; sympathetic increases rate, force and output; parasympathetic decreases rate, conduction and output; adrenal medullary hormones increase output.
Disorders: BP 120/80 normal, 140/90 hypertension; CAD deposits of calcium, fat, cholesterol, fibrous tissue; angina = chest pain from low O<sub>2</sub>; heart failure ≠ cardiac arrest ≠ heart attack.
